title: Foreign Investors Have Pulled $30 Billion From India This Year. It Is the Largest Exit in the Country's History.
excerpt: Nine straight sessions of selling, a war-driven oil shock, and a rupee under pressure. The foreign money that powered India's bull run is leaving. Here is what every NRI with Indian exposure needs to know.
body:
The numbers are no longer abstract. Foreign portfolio investors have sold a record $30.4 billion worth of Indian equities since January, making 2026 the worst year for foreign capital in the country's market history. On Wednesday alone, FPIs offloaded shares worth Rs 2,125 crore, marking a ninth consecutive session of outflows — and the selling shows no sign of stopping.

The Nifty 50 has fallen 7.8 per cent since the Iran conflict began at the end of February. The Sensex is down 9 per cent. For NRI investors who poured money into Indian markets during the bull run of 2023-2025, the reversal has been sharp, painful, and structurally different from previous corrections.

## What Is Driving the Exit

Three forces are operating simultaneously, and none of them is under India's control.

The Iran war, now in its fourth month, has pushed Brent crude to $94 a barrel. For India, the world's third-largest oil importer, every dollar increase in oil prices widens the current account deficit, pressures the rupee, and feeds inflation. On Wednesday night, the United States launched fresh strikes against multiple Iranian targets, and Iran retaliated with missile and drone attacks on American bases in Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain — one of the biggest escalations since the ceasefire collapsed in April. Brent surged another 1.1 per cent overnight.

The second force is American interest rates. Data released overnight showed US consumer inflation rose at its fastest pace in three years in May, boosted by surging energy prices. The Federal Reserve now has every reason to keep rates unchanged well into 2027. Higher US rates make emerging market equities less attractive for global fund managers — why take on India risk for uncertain returns when American treasuries yield over 5 per cent with no currency risk?

The third is the unwinding of a structural trade that powered India's outperformance for four years. From 2021 to mid-2025, record domestic inflows through systematic investment plans insulated Indian markets from foreign selling. But even that pillar is weakening. Equity mutual fund inflows fell 40 per cent in May to Rs 22,908 crore, the lowest in about a year. Gold ETFs saw their first outflows in twelve months as investors booked profits.

## The Domestic Cushion Is Thinning

The SIP book — Rs 30,954 crore in May — remains the one genuinely reassuring number. Retail India is still investing through automatic monthly transfers, and that structural discipline has prevented the kind of panic selling that hit Indian markets during the 2008 crisis or the taper tantrum of 2013.

But SIP resilience cannot compensate indefinitely for the scale of foreign selling. Thirteen of sixteen major sectors declined on Wednesday. Metal shares lost 1.7 per cent on fresh geopolitical fears. Midcap and smallcap indices, which had been outperforming benchmarks through the first quarter, are now underperforming as foreign and domestic flows both weaken at the margins.

The one bright spot is banking. Financial stocks rose 0.2 per cent on Wednesday, extending the previous session's gains, boosted by the RBI's concessional forex swap facility. The facility lowers the cost of mobilising foreign-currency deposits — effectively a policy tool to stem dollar outflows through the banking channel. Private bank stocks rose 0.7 per cent.

## What It Means for NRI Investors

For NRIs with portfolios in Indian equities, the calculus has shifted. The thesis that powered the last four years — strong domestic flows, a young demographic dividend, and India's relative insulation from global shocks — is being tested on every front.

The rupee has weakened to 95.35 per dollar, eroding returns for anyone measuring performance in dollars, pounds, or euros. A stock that is flat in rupee terms has already lost over 6 per cent in dollar terms this year purely from currency depreciation.

G. Chokkalingam, founder and head of research at Equinomics Research, said the benchmarks may struggle to rise much "unless foreign outflows reverse and pressure from oil, fertiliser and gold imports eases, which are all contingent on the resolution of the war."

That is the uncomfortable truth. The single biggest driver of the current selloff is a war that India has no role in and no leverage over. Until Brent crude drops meaningfully below $80, until the Fed signals rate cuts, and until FPI flows turn positive, the risk-reward for adding Indian equity exposure favours patience over conviction.

## The Structural Case Has Not Changed

None of this invalidates the long-term India story. GDP growth remains above 6 per cent. Corporate earnings in banking, consumer discretionary, and infrastructure are still expanding. The digital payments ecosystem continues to deepen, and the government's capital expenditure programme is the largest in Indian history.

But structural stories need cyclical patience. NRI investors who are dollar-cost-averaging into Indian mutual funds through SIPs should continue — the discipline works precisely because it buys more units when prices are low. Those sitting on concentrated positions in midcap or smallcap Indian stocks should review their exposure and ensure they can withstand another 10-15 per cent drawdown without distress.

The $30 billion question is not whether India will recover. It is whether the NRI investor has the liquidity and the temperament to hold through what may be the deepest foreign capital drought the country has ever faced.

*Sources: Reuters; The Hindu BusinessLine; Equinomics Research; AMFI data for May 2026*
